extra.message: The `expr` query parameter is passed directly to `eval()`. Although `__builtins__` is emptied, this is not a security boundary — Python sandbox escapes via object introspection (e.g. `().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()`) are well known, allowing arbitrary code execution on the server.
The `host` query parameter is concatenated into a shell command string executed with `os.system()`. A value such as `127.0.0.1; rm -rf /` or `$(curl attacker)` yields arbitrary OS command execution.

The `fragment` query parameter is concatenated into a Jinja2 template source string that is then compiled and rendered. Attacker-supplied template syntax is executed server-side (SSTI), which in Jinja2 escalates to remote code execution via the object/config traversal gadgets.

The uploaded file's client-supplied `file.filename` is passed to `os.path.splitext()` and the resulting 'extension' is appended to the generated name without sanitisation. `splitext` only splits on the last dot, so a filename like `x.pdf/../../../../etc/cron.d/pwn` yields an extension containing path separators and `..` segments; `os.path.join(settings.UPLOAD_DIR, safe_name)` then resolves outside the upload directory, allowing an authenticated borrower to write arbitrary attacker-controlled bytes to arbitrary filesystem locations.

cwe: CWE-73: External Control of File Name or Path

extra.message: The `packet_ref` query parameter is joined onto `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` with no canonicalisation or containment check, then read. `?packet_ref=../../../../etc/passwd` (or an absolute path, which `pathlib` `/` honours) reads arbitrary files from the server filesystem.

The `name` query parameter selects the write target under `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` with no canonicalisation, allowlist, or containment check, and `mkdir(parents=True)` even creates intermediate directories. `?name=../../../../root/.ssh/authorized_keys` writes attacker-controlled request body bytes to an arbitrary path.

cwe: CWE-73: External Control of File Name or Path

extra.message: An `lxml.etree.XMLParser` is explicitly constructed with `load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True` and `no_network=False`, then used to parse the raw request body. This enables XML External Entity attacks: local file disclosure (`SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"`), SSRF via network entities, and billion-laughs style denial of service.

cwe: CWE-611: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference

extra.message: The `url` query parameter is fetched with `urllib.request.urlopen()` with no scheme allowlist, host allowlist, or private/link-local address filtering, and the response body is returned to the caller. This is a full read-SSRF: internal services and cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254) can be reached and their contents exfiltrated; `file://` URLs also read local files.

The raw JSON request body (or its `filter` key) is passed unvalidated as the MongoDB query document to `find_one()`. An attacker can inject query operators such as `{"$ne": null}`, `{"$gt": ""}` or `{"$where": "..."}` to bypass intended filtering and read arbitrary records.

cwe: CWE-943: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic

extra.message: The status-transition block applies the same `VALID_TRANSITIONS` table to every role. A borrower is permitted to edit their own application while it is in `counteroffered` state (line 202), and `VALID_TRANSITIONS[counteroffered]` includes `approved`. A borrower can therefore PUT `{"status": "approved"}` on their own application and self-approve their loan, bypassing underwriter authority entirely. The same gap lets a support_specialist (allowed to change `status` at lines 207-212) drive `in_review` to `approved`.

`GET /api/integrations/status/{app_id}` has no `Depends(require_user)` and no API-key verification, unlike every other endpoint in the application. Any unauthenticated caller can enumerate `app_id` values and learn the status and update time of every loan application in the system, including whether a given application was approved or rejected.

extra.message: The privilege decision is made purely from a client-supplied `ops_badge` cookie or `x-ops-badge` header. Any caller who sets the header to `lead` receives the elevated response containing payroll and casework data; no server-side identity or policy state is consulted.

cwe: CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision

extra.message: The entire client JSON body is merged into the server-side workset dict with `dict.update()`, letting the caller overwrite security-relevant fields such as `role`, `tier`, `approved` and `balance`. The same pattern appears at line 50, where `state` is taken straight from the payload.

cwe: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

extra.message: The `card` query parameter is rendered through Jinja2's `|safe` filter, explicitly disabling autoescaping, and returned as `text/html`. `?card=<script>...</script>` executes attacker JavaScript in the victim's browser against this origin (reflected XSS).

The `lane` query parameter is used directly as the target of a `RedirectResponse` with no allowlist or same-origin check. `?lane=https://evil.example/login` produces a redirect from a trusted lending-portal URL to an attacker site, enabling credential phishing.

cwe: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site

extra.message: The request's `Origin` header is reflected verbatim into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` while `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is set to `true`. Any website can therefore issue credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint and read the response, defeating the same-origin policy for authenticated sessions.

cwe: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains

extra.message: `ssl._create_unverified_context()` is used for an outbound HTTPS call to a partner endpoint, disabling both certificate chain and hostname verification. A network attacker can transparently man-in-the-middle the connection and forge partner responses.

`response.set_cookie("portal_crumb", marker)` is called with attacker-controlled data and without `httponly`, `secure`, or `samesite` flags, so the cookie is readable by JavaScript and transmitted over cleartext HTTP.
The handler explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and an empty `Content-Security-Policy`, deliberately disabling browser-side XSS and injection mitigations for this response.

cwe: CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers

extra.message: The verifier check distinguishes an unknown handle (404 'unknown handle') from a valid handle with a wrong verifier (403 'bad verifier'), allowing enumeration of valid handles. The secret comparison itself uses `!=` rather than a constant-time comparison, and there is no attempt limiting on the 4-digit verifier, so it can be brute-forced.

cwe: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

extra.message: The login endpoint performs an unlimited number of password verifications per account. There is no per-IP or per-account rate limiting, no lockout after repeated failures, no CAPTCHA, and no such control in any middleware — `main.py` registers only `CORSMiddleware`. Credentials on this lending portal can be brute-forced or credential-stuffed at will. The same absence applies to `/password-reset-confirm` (line 76), where the 32-byte reset token can be guessed without throttling, and to `/password-reset-request` (line 64), which can be abused for unlimited reset-mail generation.

cwe: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

extra.message: Failed authentication raises HTTP 401 without any call to `log_audit`, while successful logins are logged at line 50. Authentication failures therefore produce no durable audit record anywhere in the request path (no logging middleware or exception handler exists in `main.py`), making password-guessing and credential-stuffing campaigns invisible to detection and forensics. The same omission applies to password reset requests (lines 63-72, no audit entry) and to every 403 authorization rejection across the routers.

The JWT signing key defaults to the hardcoded literal `change-me-in-production-32-char-long-key`, and the same value is baked into `docker-compose.yml` (line 21) as the container's `SECRET_KEY`. Anyone with access to this source can forge HS256 access tokens for any `sub` (user id), including admin accounts, achieving complete authentication bypass. The database password is likewise hardcoded on line 5.

cwe: CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource

extra.message: Every borrower account created by the CSV import is assigned the same hardcoded password `TempPass123!`, with no forced reset, no expiry, and no email verification. Since account emails come from the CSV (and borrower emails are otherwise discoverable), an attacker who knows this constant can log in as any imported borrower and access their loan applications, SSNs, and financial documents.

The `access_token` session cookie is set with `secure=False`, so the JWT is transmitted over plaintext HTTP. A network attacker on the same path can capture the token and fully impersonate the user for the 8-hour token lifetime. `samesite="lax"` also leaves top-level cross-site GET navigations authenticated.

Internal underwriting rationale — deliberately modelled as a separate column from the borrower-facing `reasons` — is therefore disclosed to the loan applicant, unlike internal notes and messages which are correctly filtered by `is_internal` elsewhere.
